bodyHtml:
What’s new in Java 26 release

Everything about the latest Java 26 release and infamous project Valhalla

Java 26 released on March 17, 2026. 10 JEPs. Five final, four preview, one incubator. No new stable language features this time but there are performance improvements that cost you zero code changes, a preview feature that’s been cooking for four rounds and is almost ready, and one removal that was 10 years overdue.

Here’s what actually matters.

HTTP/3 in the standard library

The HttpClient API has been around since Java 11. Java 26 adds HTTP/3 support to it.

HTTP/3 runs on QUIC instead of TCP, faster handshakes, no head-of-line blocking, better on unreliable networks. Already used by most browsers and ~40% of websites. Before this, if you needed it in Java, you were adding third-party libs.

HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_3)
    .build();

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.example.com/data"))
    .GET()
    .build();

HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(
    request,
    HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
);

That’s it. No extra config, no dependencies.

AOT Cache now works with any GC

Java 24 introduced the Ahead-of-Time (AOT) cache which is a way to pre-load and pre-initialize classes from a training run so the JVM doesn’t cold-start every time. The catch: it only worked with the G1 garbage collector, because objects were stored in a G1-specific format.

Java 26 fixes that. The cache format is now GC-agnostic, so it works with ZGC too.

If you’re running latency-sensitive workloads and already using ZGC for low-pause GC, you now also get faster startup. Previously you had to pick one.

G1 GC throughput improvement

G1 has been the default GC since Java 9. The way it works is moving live objects between memory regions concurrently with your app — requires constant synchronization between app threads and GC threads. That synchronization has always been a quiet overhead tax. JEP 522 reduces that synchronization significantly.

Your throughput goes up. You change nothing. Just upgrade the JDK.

final is fixed finally

This is a future-proofing warning, not a breaking change yet.

Java has always allowed you to bypass final fields using deep reflectionfield.setAccessible(true) then field.set(obj, newValue). Frameworks have relied on this for years.

Field field = MyClass.class.getDeclaredField("CONSTANT");
field.setAccessible(true);
field.set(null, "mutated");
// WARNING: Reflective mutation of final field MyClass.CONSTANT

Java 26 now warns you when this happens. A future version will block it entirely. If you maintain any library that does this, start planning.

The Applet API is Gone

Deprecated since Java 17. Removed in Java 26. If you still have import java.applet.* in production code, that's a separate conversation.

Preview Features

These aren’t production-ready, but they’re where Java is heading.

To use preview features:

# Compile
javac --enable-preview --release 26 MyApp.java

# Run
java --enable-preview MyApp

With Maven:

<compilerArgs>
  <arg>--enable-preview</arg>
</compilerArgs>
<source>26</source>
<target>26</target>

Primitive Types in Patterns (4th Preview)

Pattern matching in Java currently doesn’t work cleanly with primitive types. You can match on Integer, String, any object but not directly on int, long, double. JEP 530 changes that.

Before:

Object value = getSomeValue();

if (value instanceof Integer i) {
    if (i >= 0 && i <= 100) {
        System.out.println("In range: " + i);
    }
}

After JEP 530:

// --enable-preview --release 26

switch (value) {
    case int i when i >= 0 && i <= 100 -> System.out.println("In range: " + i);
    case int i -> System.out.println("Out of range: " + i);
    case String s -> System.out.println("String: " + s);
    default -> System.out.println("Something else");
}

This is its fourth preview. The changes between rounds have been small. It’s close to final.

Structured Concurrency (6th Preview)

Virtual threads landed in Java 21. Structured Concurrency is the API that makes them actually ergonomic.

The idea: if you’re running multiple concurrent tasks as part of one logical operation, they should be scoped together. If one fails, the others should be cancelled automatically. No thread leaks, no manual cleanup.

// --enable-preview --release 26

try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
    Supplier<String> user        = scope.fork(() -> fetchUser(userId));
    Supplier<List<Order>> orders = scope.fork(() -> fetchOrders(userId));

    scope.join().throwIfFailed();

    return new UserDashboard(user.get(), orders.get());
}

If fetchUser throws, fetchOrders gets cancelled. The scope closes cleanly. This is what concurrent code should look like.

Lazy Constants (2nd Preview)

Previously called “Stable Values.” The rename is more accurate, these are values computed once, on first access, treated as constants by the JVM from that point on.

// --enable-preview --release 26

class Config {
    static final LazyConstant<String> DB_URL = LazyConstant.of(
        () -> System.getenv("DATABASE_URL")
    );
}

The JIT compiler can optimize these more aggressively than regular fields because it knows the value will never change after initialization. Useful in config-heavy, framework-style code.

The Valhalla Setup

Java 26 is a smaller release than usual. That’s deliberate.

Lazy Constants, Primitive Types in Patterns, the GC-agnostic AOT format , a lot of this reads like groundwork. The language model is being cleaned up to make space for something bigger.

Project Valhalla is Java’s long-running effort to add value types, classes without identity that the JVM can treat like primitives. Flat memory layout, no heap allocation overhead, no pointer indirection. The missing piece between int (fast) and Integer (boxed, slow at scale).

Valhalla EA builds are already downloadable through IntelliJ IDEA. The first preview features are expected in Java 27 (September 2026).

When they land, it’ll be the biggest change to how Java handles data-intensive code since Generics.

Conclusion

Java 26 isn’t trying to be dramatic. The G1 and AOT improvements alone make the upgrade worth it for most teams, and the Valhalla groundwork means Java 27 is going to be a much bigger story.
